I just finished "The War of Art" by Steven Pressfield. It is a great non fiction about the struggles artists/musicians/athletes face in order to make a living and get their work noticed. The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains by Nicholas Carr

Some neat insights into how media (from the printed word [and its evolution from tablet to paper to scroll to bound book] to google results) — specifically the internet — not only affects how (and, to a degree, what) we think, but also how it physically changes our brains.

I'm actually reading it again, even though I just finished it on Thursday... partially because I don't have anything else to read at the moment, but also because I only read on the train so I tend to read books more than once just to absorb them more thoroughly.

Also, right before this one I read The Filter Bubble by Eli Pariser which would have probably made more sense to read after The Shallows. They cover semi-related topics — The Shallows being more about the general evolution of absorbing information through our eyes via words and how different media affects our ability to do so (which directly trains us what to think), while The Filter Bubble is more about how the internet, the personalization of the internet specifically, is affecting how and what we think. Personally, I kinda think it's ushering in a new era of highly-fractured tribalism....

Which, oddly enough, ties into another book I've read recently. In Guns, Germs, and Steel it talks about how both the early unification of China and the highly-fractured nature of groups of tribes were disadvantages that were both partially responsible for giving Europe — which had just the right amount of unity and opposition — an advantage in the old world.
